newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan shilling sinks to all-time low on dollar.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan shilling sinks to all-time low on dollar.

text.p: Kenya's shilling sank to an official record low against the dollar on Thursday and the government declared illegal a national strike called for Friday, raising chances of violent clashes.
On the industrial front, a go-slow by Kenyan air traffic controllers ended with agreement with the government and flights returned to normal after five days of cancellations and delays.

On a slide since the International Monetary Fund halted a key aid package last week citing corruption, the shilling hit a commercial average of 70.2 against the dollar at 2 p.m. (1100 GMT) from Wednesday's close of 67.50, a decline of four percent.
The shilling's last official low against the dollar was 69.22 in October 1993.

Commercial dealers said investors were alarmed by President Daniel arap Moi on Tuesday playing down the IMF ruling and urging Kenyans to become self-reliant. He also said the lost IMF loans were insignificant compared to Kenya's whole economy.
Moi, 73, and in power for 19 years, has yet to name a date for a general election which must be held this year.
The shilling low was reached despite Central Bank of Kenya Governor Micah Cheserem appealing for an end to panic in the foreign exchange market as some foreign investors pulled out.
Worries in the foreign exchange market were compounded by a call by an opposition-backed alliance of groups demanding constitutional reforms for a national general strike on Friday.
Labour Minister Philip Masinde on Thursday declared the strike illegal and urged police to ensure Friday was normal.
"The strike is going to be unlawful and it is an offence to participate in such activities, just as it is unlawful for anyone to incite workers to go out on strike," he told a news conference.
"I would like to advise as well as appeal to the workers all over the country not to take the law into their own hands, to ignore the strike call and continue to do their work," he said.
"I urged the security (police) to take all measures to ensure the day passes as normal, to stop any activities that may be termed illegal," he added.
Masinde's statement appeared to set the stage for clashes on Friday between reform supporters and riot police as the strike organisers have called for marches in support of the stoppage.
The United Nations said its offices in central Nairobi would be closed on Friday and buses that usually take most of its employees to offices outside the city centre would not run.

At least nine people were killed on July 7 during clashes between police and pro-reform demonstrators in Nairobi and other centres. The worst political violence in seven years rattled investors and tourists.
Moi's government has offered a set of minimal changes before the elections and a constitutional review after the elections and has managed to dent opposition support for the strike.
"It is obvious that it (strike) will put the workers in trouble with their employers with the likely consequences of being dismissed from their jobs," the labour minister said.
Masinde said the government could not discount incidents of violence breaking out on Friday as a few people were bent on breaking the law. He added that police would be vigilant.
At the same news conference, Masinde announced the go-slow by Kenyan air traffic controllers since Saturday had ended.
"The situation is back to normal. We have explained what the government is trying to do and they (controllers) have understood and cooperated," he said but did not give details.

Air controllers told Reuters they returned to normal work after being assured that a report presented to Moi on Wednesday on the terms and conditions of service for government workers would meet their concerns.

They said the head of the civil service had assured them on Thursday that details of the report would be released in two weeks. They said if the promises fell short of their demands they would either resume the go-slow or start another action.
"We will see if it meets our expectations," said an air controller at Moi International Airport in the city of Mombasa.
The air traffic controllers had demanded a 50-fold increase in what they say is pay of about $90 a month, plus benefits.
